grammar[0].fact: German health insurance is compulsory, and most people are in a public fund, whose cost your employer shares. A hospital stay costs you only a small charge per day. Complaining about the rolls is free.

document.intro: A real plaque on a hospital wall in Hamburg. It is one single sentence, of the kind Germans only write on walls. The whole life is in a relative clause: *der sich … erworben hat*. Find the dates first.
document.fact: German hospitals are often named after a saint, a city or a donor, and they are full of plaques. *Verdienste erwerben* is plaque language: to earn merit. Nobody says it aloud, unless they’re on their way to a retirement party.
document.tasks[1].instruction: Complete with um … zu or damit.
reading.intro: Herr Yilmaz the baker has broken his leg. He gets up at four every day of his life, and now he’s on a ward, and it is four o’clock. The night nurse on the ward is Lena, who knows him from the courtyard.
reading.fact: Germany has a lot of hospital beds, more per head than almost any comparable country, and patients stay longer. They also wake up early: the breakfast round at six or seven is a national experience. Bring your own slippers, towel and pyjamas: the hospital generally won’t provide them.
